titleStmt.title: The Secretary of Defense (Marshall) to the Secretary of State

div.head: The Secretary of Defense (Marshall) to the Secretary of State
div.p: Dear Mr. Secretary: With reference to your letter of 15 November 1950 regarding proposed United States-United Kingdom-French military talks concerning the defense of Indochina, I am transmitting herewith, for your information, a memorandum of 10 January 1951 from the Joint Chiefs of Staff on this subject. In this memorandum the Joint Chiefs of Staff refer to a previous memorandum to me, dated 8 December 1950, in which they then stated that “additional military staff talks should not be undertaken at this time.” I am also enclosing that memorandum for your information.

In view of the opinion which the Joint Chiefs of Staff have reaffirmed in their memorandum of 10 January 1951 that, from the strictly military point of view, no additional military staff talks are desirable at this time, I believe that the holding of such talks now depends on whether or not the Department of State believes that there are overriding political considerations. I realize that the opinion of the Joint Chiefs of Staff would have the effect of indefinitely postponing your agreement reached with Mr. Schuman and Mr. Bevin
on 14 September 1950. Yet, I believe that, in the light of the views of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the Department of Defense can only recommend that, unless there are overriding political considerations, the French and British Governments be informed of the present U.S. military position regarding these talks.

note.p: Secretary of State Acheson’s letter to Secretary of Defense Marshall, November 15, 1950, not printed, suggested that preparations be completed for the earliest possible meeting of high military officers of the United States, the United Kingdom, and France regarding Indochina (790.5/11–1550). For documentation on the question of staff talks, see Foreign Relations, 1950, vol, vi, pp. 690 ff.

At a meeting on September 14, 1950, Secretary Acheson informed Robert Schuman, French Foreign Minister, and Ernest Bevin, British Foreign Secretary, that the United States wished to commence military staff talks on Indochina. For documentation on consideration of Indochina at the New York Tripartite Foreign Ministers meeting, September 12–14 and 18–19, 1950, see Foreign Relations, 1950, vol. vi, pp. 880 ff.
